item.title: The Billionaire's Tax Loophole That Lets You Borrow Money Without Paying Tax
item.description: The ultra-wealthy have a clever financial strategy known as the "buy, borrow, die" loophole to avoid paying income taxes. First, billionaires purchase massive amounts of appreciating assets like stocks or corporate shares. Instead of selling these assets to get cash, which would trigger capital gains taxes, they use them as collateral for loans. Because the government does not view borrowed money as income, these loans are entirely tax-free. This allows wealthy individuals to fund lavish lifestyles and major investments without reporting taxable earnings. When the asset owner dies, the investments are transferred to heirs with an updated tax basis that erases previous gains. Critics argue this system creates an unfair burden on regular workers who pay taxes on every paycheck. To fix this imbalance, Congress recently introduced legislation like the ROBINHOOD Act to target these asset-backed loans. This proposed law aims to eliminate the loophole by taxing large loans backed by financial portfolios. https://www.gallego.senate.gov/news/press-releases/gallego-introduces-legislation-to-crack-down-on-billionaire-tax-loophole/

item.title: NYC's New Mayor Says He Found A $12 Billion Deficit When He Took Office, Double What The Previous Administration Admitted
item.description: https://www.reddit.com/r/BoredPandaHQ/s/7QwraTj1aV https://www.factcheckradar.com/fact-check/mamdani-erases-12-billion-deficit-in-first-budget According to official statements from the NYC Mayor's Office and reporting from multiple news outlets, Mayor Zohran Mamdani inherited a budget deficit exceeding $12 billion. During his budget presentation on May 12, 2026, the Mayor confirmed that this gap had been reduced in stages, first to $5.4 billion and finally to zero. This fiscal turnaround was made possible by a significant partnership with Governor Kathy Hochul, who secured nearly $8 billion in state assistance over two years to stabilize the city's finances. The balanced budget relies on several new fiscal strategies, including a projected $500 million annually from a new pied-à-terre tax on non-resident second homes valued over $5 million, as well as $1.47 billion in agency savings. However, the methods used to reach this zero-dollar balance have drawn sharp criticism. Reports indicate that a significant portion of the 'state aid' involves 'kick-the-can' measures, such as restructuring $2.2 billion in pension plan payments and delaying mandates for school class sizes. Critics, including the Citizens Budget Commission, have labeled these as 'pension gimmicks' and 'temporary plugs' that may exacerbate future fiscal problems. While the current deficit has been eliminated on paper for the upcoming fiscal year, city Comptroller Mark Levine warned that the reliance on one-shot measures could lead to a $7 billion shortfall by 2028. Political opponents have also characterized the initial deficit warnings as 'tactical chess' or 'performative' theater designed to pressure the state for funding. Despite these long-term concerns and political debates over the methods, the immediate claim regarding the elimination of the inherited $12 billion deficit is accurate based on the executive budget release. Source quality: The report is based on an official press release from the NYC Mayor's Office and corroborating reports from multiple reputable news outlets, including CBS New York, amNewYork, and the New York Post, all dated May 12, 2026. These sources provide both the official figures and critical analysis of the budget's sustainability.
